Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds, Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Tariq was forty when the mortar struck the neighborhood square, but the memory of that day still folds over him like a sudden drop in temperature. He had been buying olives from a roadside vendor when the first whistle tore through the morning air, followed immediately by the wet, heavy thud of impact against the packed earth. Dirt erupted in thick, dark plumes, coating his jacket and settling into the creases of his collar. Men shouted each other’s names over the ringing in his ears, and he found himself gripping a lamppost, listening to the sharp, metallic crack of shrapnel biting into concrete. The scent of crushed soil and damp stone clung to him long after he returned home. He did not know it then, but those particular sounds, that thick outdoor earthiness, and the way strangers called out names he would later hear repeated in his sleep, had already become the anchors of his alarm. In the weeks that followed, Tariq began to map his days around what felt safe. He stopped walking through the city parks. The smell of turning soil and damp grass pressed against him, a tangible reminder of the ground that had just given way beneath him. He started taking the subway instead of walking, favoring the underground where the air was filtered and the familiar rumble of trains felt less like artillery and more like a steady, predictable heartbeat. When he heard his wife’s brother say his own name during a phone call, or caught a radio broadcaster mentioning the names of the neighborhoods where he had once lived during the strikes, he would pause mid-step, certain the words carried a weight they did not seem to hold for anyone else. His marriage remained intact, yet something shifted in how he moved through their shared kitchen and living room. He had come to believe he was dead inside, a quiet certainty that showed in the way he sat through dinner without tasting his food, his hands resting flat on the table, his expressions flattened into a steady, untroubled line. He had lost his faith in people, life, or a higher power, and the ritual simply felt unfamiliar now. At forty-one, Tariq returned to his work as a dancer, but the studio had become both refuge and trap. He spent his evenings on the sprung wooden floor, rehearsing contemporary pieces under the high windows. Yet the mirrors above the barre felt less like reflections and more like interrogations. He felt that others could see what happened to him just by looking at him, and he would often turn his shoulder away from the glass during group stretches, adjusting his posture as if trying to make himself smaller. The consequence of this vigilance accumulated quietly: he began skipping social performances after rehearsals, telling his wife he needed to stretch out the pain, though the real reason was the sensation of dozens of eyes tracing the same invisible patterns across his shoulders that he felt everyone could already read. His avoidance had grown into a habit, then a quiet separation from the very community that once animated his art. It was the accumulation of these small, persistent withdrawals that finally brought him to the clinic. He had noticed that the deadness in his chest no longer felt like rest but like a waiting room, and the fear of being truly seen had begun to bleed into his dance. What he hoped for now was not the erasure of the past, but a way to move through the world without bracing for the next crack in the air or the next gust of familiar earth. He sat in the intake chair, listening to the therapist’s voice, aware that the sound of a passing siren and the faint, outdoor scent of rain on pavement were already settling into his coat, already making sense.
